Definition:Characters are central to narrative writing. We want to create real characters: characters that live and breathe and act in believable ways, and most importantly characters whom our readers will find worth caring about. Just like real creatures, characters have strengths and weaknesses, and they have specific personalities (p.31).

Characters are the person represented in a dramatic or narrative work who are interpreted by the reader, as processing particular, moral intellectual, and emotional qualities by inferences, from what the persons say and their distinctive way of saying—the dialogue——and from what they do----the action.
Character may remain essentially "stable," or unchanged in outlook and disposition, from beginning to the end of the work (Prospero in Shakespeare’s The Tempest, Micawber in Charles Dickens’s David Copperfield), or may undergo radical change, either through a gradual process of development, (the title character in Jane Austen's Emma), or as a result of the crisis (Shakespeare’s, King Lear; Pip in Dickens’ Great Expectations) (2014:91)
Cengage Learning
A Glossary of
Literary Terms

Albus Dumbledore
Headmaster Albus Dumbledore: His first name is from the Latin word alba, “white.” His last name, according to Rowling interviews, is Old English for “bumblebee.” In color symbolism, white often stands for purity, so the headmaster’s name suggests honor and a hard-working nature (“busy as a bee”).

pages.html:
Sirius Black
Sirius Black: His first name is the "Dog Star," brightest in the Canis Major (Great Dog) constellation. There are at least two three stars in the Sirius system, and the brightest is Sirius A; it is 10 times brighter than our sun. This star was given god status among the ancient Egyptians and later the Greeks. The dog represented by the constellation was the faithful companion to Orion the hunter, who also is a constellation. Appropriate for a wizard who can transform into a dog. Black suggests the dark nature that wizards unaware of Sirius' innocence assign to him. It also could suggest "black dog," the form he takes when his uses his skill as an Animagus.

pages.html: The passage is a tour through the five senses. Mann lets us see: a narrow room, a high ceiling, rows of hams and sausages, canned preserves, and translucent glass bottles. He lets us smell: the fragrance of chocolate and smoked fish and earthy truffles. He lets us hear: “Good day,” unnatural tones died away in the stillness. He lets us taste: to water like a spring. He lets us touch: grab, slipped a fistful into my coat pocket. The writing is alive because Mann lets us perceive the scene as we would live it, through our sense perceptions

pages.html: My throat tightened. I stared at the lines of the wooden floor beneath us, tracing their uneven grain.I opened my mouth, but nothing came. Not even the smallest breath of what I needed to say. She didn’t know—how could she?—the weight of the silence I carried. The things I couldn’t speak, the things that had no name. The language she used, the precise and measured way she laid out her pain, it was foreign to me. Each time she spoke, it felt like a demand I could never meet. I wanted to answer, to explain why I couldn’t meet her eyes, why the space between us had become so vast, but—Her words rang in my head, overlapping with my own thoughts, drowning them. How could I tell her that I wasn’t withholding out of cruelty or spite? That this silence wasn’t a weapon, wasn’t a wall meant to push her away, but rather something that wrapped itself tightly around me, suffocating any chance of an honest response? The truth lived somewhere deep within me, too tangled in fear to surface.

The family dinner dragged on, and Charlie, as always, dominated the conversation with his wild tales. He leaned back, laughing, recounting yet another story of how he'd "put his boss in his place." The room was filled with forced smiles, nods, and uneasy silence.
Across the table, Sarah had had enough. She put down her fork. “Charlie, how many jobs have you lost this year?”
Charlie blinked, caught off guard. “That’s not the point—”
“No,” Sarah said quietly, “it is the point. When are you going to stop pretending it’s always someone else’s fault?”
The room froze. Charlie said nothing. Sarah had finally spoken the truth everyone else had been too afraid to say.

I’m sorry, but the leaves are falling again,” she said, her voice soft, almost lost in the wind that rustled through the dry, brittle branches above.
He looked at her, hands deep in his coat pockets, eyes squinting against the amber light of late afternoon. “They fall every year. What do you expect them to do—hold on forever?”
“No, I don’t expect that,” she said, her gaze following the lazy drift of a red-brown leaf. “I just… I thought this year might be different. I thought maybe things wouldn’t slip away so easily.”
He sighed, the weight of her words settling like the coming dusk. “Nothing stays the same. Not the leaves, not us.”
“I know,” she replied, her breath fogging in the cold air. “But it feels like everything’s falling at once this time. More than the leaves. More than just the season.”
He kicked at the ground, stirring a pile of them, the crunch loud in the silence between them. “It’s just change. You get used to it.”
“Do you?” she asked, her voice barely more than a whisper. “Do you get used to watching everything drift away? Because I don’t think I can.”

pages.html:
He didn’t answer at first, just stood there, the fading light casting long shadows between them. “I’m not sure you’re supposed to get used to it. Maybe that’s the point.”
She turned to him, her eyes dark with unshed tears. “Then what do you do? If you don’t get used to it, if things just keep slipping away, what do you hold on to?”
He finally looked at her, and his voice softened, as though the wind might carry it away too. “Maybe you hold on to the fact that it’s not about keeping everything. It’s about seeing it when it’s there. Knowing that it’s there, even if only for a moment.”
She bit her lip, fighting the quiver that wanted to rise. “But what if I need more than a moment?”
He smiled, a sad smile, the kind you give when you’ve lived through too many seasons. “Then you’ve got to learn to make those moments last longer in your heart than they do on the branch.”
They stood there, the world around them slowly letting go, but for a while—just a while—they held on to the words that fell between them like the leaves that kept tumbling from the trees.

things just keep slipping away, what do you hold on to?”

He finally looked at her, and his voice softened, as though the wind might carry it away too. “Maybe you 
hold on to the fact that it’s not about keeping everything. It’s about seeing it when it’s there. Knowing 
that it’s there, even if only for a moment.”
She bit her lip, fighting the quiver that wanted to rise. “But what if I need more than a moment?”

He smiled, a sad smile, the kind you give when you’ve lived through too many seasons. “Then you’ve got 
to learn to make those moments last longer in your heart than they do on the branch.”

They stood there, the world around them slowly letting go, but for a while—just a while—they held on 
to the words that fell between them like the leaves that kept tumbling from the trees.
